newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed sharply higher inspired by the surprisingly large draw in US certified coffee stocks. Traders said growing worries over Colombian supplies following a prolonged strike by truck drivers also lent a bullish tone to the market.

The most active November/January spread, a barometer of nearby supply availability, stood at $122 at the close after touching a high of $143, as funds sold January to cover their short positions in November. January closed $40 higher at $1,427 a tonne while November firmed $49 to close at $1,549.

In New York the December/March spread exploded to 11 cents/lb. December added 4.60 cents/lb to close at 117.60 cents/lb, while March closed 2.55 cents/lb higher at 106.60 cents/lb. The outer months added 1.35 to 1.75 cents/lb.
The rally was in response to the steep reduction in certified coffee stocks which fell 24,391 60-kg bags in the week ended October 18 to 5,583 bags.
But what was seen as more bullish is that no coffee was pending certification, greatly diminishing chances for a build in stocks next week.

Some traders said the strong market reaction to the stock news could be more psychological than anything as the numbers do not mean very much. It was added if the market trades about 100 million bags a year, then 25,000 bags do not really make a big difference. The December/March spread should be wide enough to attract some coffee, traders said, but the pipeline is rather empty so the wide spread might not be able to draw in supplies and it might be simply a matter of timing rather than price, it was added.

COLOMBIA - A week-old trucker strike paralyzed the nation's coffee industry and forced delays in the shipment of about 250,000 60-kg bags, promised for delivery to export clients in October and 25 per cent of the 1 million bags that the country had planned to export during the month, Jorge Cardenas, head of the National Coffee Growers Federation, said. He added that coffee was also unable to leave processing centers for Colombia's ports and that the industry was 'completely paralyzed.'

SOUTH KOREA - South Korea imported 494,600 bags of coffee in January/June 1996, 17 per cent less than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 7.5 per cent to 1.084 million bags. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/June 1996 were Honduras (64,600 vs 48,500 bags), Colombia (71,800 vs 73,700 bags), Indonesia (96,900 vs 41,100 bags) and Vietnam (66,600 vs 129,100 bags).

NEW ZEALAND - New Zealand imported 109,300 bags of coffee in January/August 1996, 15 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Imports in calendar year 1995 rose slightly to 149,500 bags from 148,100 bags the previous year. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/August 1996 were Indonesia (23,700 vs 25,400 bags), Vietnam (18,800 vs 15,900 bags) and Papua/New Guinea (18,000 vs 14,700 bags).
